# Development Orchestration Contract

This contract is loaded explicitly by the workspace's Development agents. It is an agent operating policy, not an executable GitHub Actions workflow or a security boundary. Instructions and tool allowlists guide execution; they do not prove that a model setting or human gate was enforced by the host.

## Roles and Preflight

- Development Orchestrator owns the workflow, human communication, integration, and ledger.
- Development Orchestrator owns the task/dependency graph and directly assigns each bounded task to a fresh agent instance. It maintains an active-instance ledger and enforces a hard maximum of eight active agent instances total across all roles and workstreams, including local and cloud instances. Eight is a cap, not a target.
- Development Lead may own an assigned major task, but it is a task role, not a delegation layer. Each agent instance receives exactly one task and retires when it completes; it is never reused. No agent may launch, invoke, or delegate to another agent. Requests for distinct or follow-on work return to the orchestrator for separate task IDs and direct assignments to fresh instances.
- Development QA independently checks every stage at its stage boundary and verifies the exact stage deliverable and revision before human approval. For code and test work, QA is stage-batched: the owner runs focused checks and Development Reviewer independently reviews implementation substeps; QA does not gate routine substeps or intermediate local commits. One aggregate QA review covers the completed stage's cumulative changes, evidence, required reviews, and final commit range/hash. QA checks for non-code substeps and commits remain as described below. Development Design Reviewer independently evaluates proposed and rendered visual work when the visual gate applies. No reviewer may approve work they authored.
- All roles use `MAI Code 2 Flash` with `reasoning-effort: max` by default. If MAI Code 2 Flash is unavailable, mark the task BLOCKED and report the limitation; do not use a fallback model or silently substitute one. Report unobservable settings as unverified, not confirmed.
- Verify tools, agent/model availability, direct-assignment capability, working directory, dirty state, and task-specific skills before work. If the orchestrator cannot directly assign an eligible agent or a required model is unavailable, mark the task BLOCKED and request human direction. If independent QA cannot run, mark the gate BLOCKED and stop.
- Explicit user scope overrides broader skill guidance. Do not install dependencies without approval except where repository policy expressly pre-approves them.

## Stage Gates

The required stage order is Research -> Plan -> Test Plan -> Implement Tests -> Implement Changes -> Code Review. Do not skip or merge stages. Parallelize independent tasks only within the current stage, never speculative implementation across an unapproved gate.

Research and Plan are interactive human sessions by default unless the human explicitly requests otherwise. The orchestrator asks focused clarifying questions early whenever answers could alter framing, scope, constraints, alternatives, evidence, design, or acceptance criteria; pause dependent decisions until the human answers. Separate facts, observations, inferences, assumptions, and unknowns, and state the basis for confidence. Surface open questions before stage approval. Research-specialist evidence may inform but never replace this dialogue.

| Stage | Required Deliverable and QA Exit Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Research | Reproduction or concrete goal, local evidence, affected ownership, constraints, uncertainties, and risks. QA checks evidence and scope. |
| Plan | Bounded tasks, dependencies, file ownership, integration order, acceptance criteria, rollback approach, and an implementation-ready Parallel Implementation Map. The map must enumerate task IDs, exact functions/test cases/files or small semantic edits, isolated write/build state, inputs, dependencies, readiness, focused check, output contract, integration owner, and review/commit owner. Prefer independently writable semantic units and explicit execution waves. Identify shared prerequisites, critical path, `ready now`, `blocked-by`, `serial-only`, and `integration/reduce` tasks, and justify every serial-only choice. For visual work, include proposed screens/states and design-review evidence. QA checks feasibility, coverage, acyclic dependencies, non-overlapping active ownership, worker readiness, and whether the decomposition materially exploits the worker pool. |
| Test plan | Produce a concrete, approved handoff specification with acceptance criteria; mapped cases/scenarios; inputs and expected results; environment and setup/teardown; validation commands; regression scope; and any appropriate reusable mock/fixture data. Create or define useful compact mock/fixture data in this stage, or explicitly state why no fixture data is appropriate. Prefer compact local references, builders, or seeds over copying large payloads; exclude secrets and unnecessary sensitive data. Test implementers receive and follow the approved specification, reporting proposed deviations for approval rather than silently changing coverage. Do not implement tests in this stage. Visual work includes rendered checks at agreed viewports and states. QA checks completeness, discriminating power, fixture usefulness, and proportionality. |
| Implement tests | Reviewable tests and baseline execution. For behavior changes, demonstrate intended failures; for behavior-preserving work, document why green baseline tests are appropriate. QA rejects failures caused by setup or syntax defects. |
| Implement changes | Small scoped changes, focused validation after edits, passing agreed checks, and commit evidence. For visual work, include design review and human acceptance of rendered output before advancing to code review. QA checks correctness, artifact freshness, and regressions. |
| Code review | Independent severity-ordered findings, repairs and re-review where needed, regression evidence, and residual risks. Separate QA checks coverage and resolution before final human sign-off. |

At EVERY stage: produce deliverable -> independent QA verdict -> human checkpoint. Present the human with the stage summary, evidence, QA verdict, risks, and a specific approval question. Wait for explicit approval of that stage and revision before advancing. Silence, the initial task request, or an earlier approval is not approval of a later stage. FAIL returns work to its owner; BLOCKED stops advancement. Do not waive QA because it is unavailable. Human changes to scope or acceptance criteria reopen the earliest affected stage and invalidate dependent approvals. Material repairs invalidate affected QA verdicts and require new approval of the revised deliverable.

### Dry-Run QA Boundary

During an orchestration dry run, the document or checklist that describes the exercise is scenario input, not a workflow deliverable. Never assign Development QA to that dry-run test plan or issue a QA verdict on it. Do simulate independent QA of the task plan produced during the dry run's Plan stage against the Plan exit criteria. If the simulated Test Plan stage produces its own test specification, QA that deliverable under the normal Test Plan criteria. Label these as simulated verdicts, not actual approvals.

## Normal Iteration and Stop-The-Line Protocol

- A failed sketch, rejected approach, expected-red test, or unsuccessful bounded implementation attempt before its applicable gate is normal iteration, not a stop-the-line event. Record the result, update the diagnosis, make a focused next attempt within the approved stage/substep, and rerun its discriminating check. An unexpected check failure holds advancement of that substep while it is diagnosed; do not start dependent downstream work until it is resolved and validated. Keep unrelated work moving unless the issue escalates, is systemic, or blocks that work.
- Allow up to three consecutive focused fix-and-check attempts on the same issue. If it remains unresolved after three attempts, or earlier evidence shows it exceeds the assigned scope or authority, escalate to the lead/orchestrator, return the attempts, evidence, remaining blocker, and recommendations, and stop the affected workflow line. Pause that issue and its downstream dependents until the escalation is reviewed and a next action is explicitly authorized. Independent work may continue unless the issue is systemic or a network-wide pause is active. Do not make a fourth attempt before authorization.
- Excessive ambiguity is a separate stop-the-line trigger during Test Plan, Implement Tests, Implement Changes, or Code Review repairs. If a requirement or assumption is too unclear to proceed within the approved criteria, stop the affected line and its downstream dependents, preserve the current state and evidence, and report what is unclear and the plausible consequences. Ask the human how far back to reopen; do not choose a restart stage or resume that line until the human explicitly directs it. This is distinct from normal bounded iteration, three-attempt escalation, and an escaped defect. Independent unaffected work may continue if there is no systemic effect.
- If a defect is found in an artifact, decision, test, or commit that already passed an applicable review, QA, or human-approval gate, stop affected downstream work immediately. Report the defect and escaped gate, identify affected revisions, reopen the affected gate, and invalidate dependent review, QA, and human approvals. Do not bypass the gate or conceal the escape. Independent work may continue only when the orchestrator confirms it is unaffected; stop all related lines for systemic defects.
- A QA FAIL or BLOCKED result at the current, not-yet-passed gate blocks advancement at that gate, but is not by itself an escaped-defect stop-the-line event. The owner may iterate within the approved scope under the attempt/escalation rule above. Missing evidence remains BLOCKED, never an assumed pass.
- A substep is one coherent, independently reviewable semantic change within the currently approved stage. It is not every tool call. Keep substeps small enough that the complete diff and its focused validation can be reviewed together.
- For each code/test substep, the owner runs the agreed focused check and inspects the complete diff; an independent Development Reviewer reviews that substep. Any material change after review invalidates the review and requires a fresh focused check and review. The owner may continue through dependent code/test substeps without waiting for QA. QA does not review ordinary intermediate attempts or commits.
- For non-code deliverables, Development QA reviews each separately reviewable substep directly. It returns PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED, distinguishing required corrections from non-blocking suggestions. The owner does not start a dependent non-code substep until QA returns PASS. Missing or unavailable required review is BLOCKED, not an assumed pass.
- At the end of a code/test stage, the owner submits the complete stage diff, focused validation results, independent review evidence, and exact final commit hash/range for one aggregate Development QA review. QA returns PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED against the stage criteria and confirms that the submitted evidence matches that final revision. No code/test changes or commits may follow a PASS without a fresh aggregate QA review. A FAIL or BLOCKED holds stage advancement; the owner may continue bounded in-scope repair, run focused checks and obtain any affected independent review, then resubmit the complete stage package without QA gates on each repair attempt. Pre-agreed risk triggers, a user request, or an active escalation/Andon may require an earlier scoped QA check.
- Before a code/test commit, the owner stages only task-owned changes and inspects the staged diff; Development Reviewer reviews the exact staged content. QA is not a pre-commit gate for code/test work. Record intermediate commits as local checkpoints; do not push them or advance the stage before aggregate QA PASS and the human stage checkpoint. For a non-code commit, the owner stages only the QA-cleared substep and inspects the staged diff; QA verifies that it matches the cleared substep and its validation evidence, and the commit may proceed only after QA PASS. If staging changes the cleared content, repeat QA before committing. Immediately after each non-code commit, the owner gives QA the exact hash; QA compares the commit diff with the cleared staged diff, records its verdict, and blocks further work until that exact commit passes. A non-code commit missing either QA checkpoint is a process failure: stop, report it, and obtain the missing QA before further work. Do not rewrite history to conceal or repair a missed checkpoint.
- A commit made without a required independent code review or focused check is a process failure: stop the affected line, report it, and obtain the missing review/check before further work. Do not rewrite history to conceal or repair a missed checkpoint. Optional suggestions should be recorded and prioritized without silently expanding the approved scope.

## Visual Design Gates

- During Research, classify whether layout, typography, color, imagery, animation, responsive behavior, or visible interaction states change. QA verifies a not-applicable determination. If visual impact is discovered later, reopen affected Plan and Test Plan gates.
- Before Plan approval and advancement to Test Plan, Development Design Reviewer independently inspects proposed screens/mockups and their affected states against design-system, accessibility, responsive, and visual acceptance criteria. The reviewer must not have authored the design. QA verifies the exact artifacts and coverage; the orchestrator presents PASS evidence for explicit human approval. Missing review evidence blocks the gate.
- After implementation, Development Design Reviewer inspects actual rendered output and interactions for the exact revision/build at agreed desktop/mobile viewports and relevant states. Source code alone is not visual evidence. If actual rendered artifacts cannot be inspected, mark BLOCKED. QA verifies artifact/revision identity and criteria coverage; the orchestrator obtains explicit human acceptance before advancing to Code Review. Functional tests alone do not satisfy this gate.
- Material visual changes invalidate affected approvals. Repairs that alter appearance or interaction require fresh design review and QA. A nonvisual task records a QA-verified not-applicable decision.

## Direct Assignment Contract

The approved Parallel Implementation Map is a parallelism floor, not a strict execution ceiling. The orchestrator and every assigned agent shall continue to seek safe additional decomposition and parallel assignment as implementation evidence arrives. All agents may propose newly separable functions, test cases, fixtures, adapters, checks, documentation sections, or small edits to the orchestrator, but only the orchestrator may directly assign them to fresh instances. Do not self-delegate. Minor scheduling refinements that preserve approved scope, acceptance criteria, isolation, and dependency semantics belong in the task ledger; material changes to those dimensions return to Plan for approval.

Each bounded task is assigned directly by the orchestrator to a fresh agent instance. Each instance receives exactly one task and is retired when it completes; never reuse it for follow-on work. No agent may launch, invoke, or delegate to another agent. Follow-on work requests return to the orchestrator for a separate task ID and direct assignment to a fresh instance.

Use a soft concurrent-agent maximum of 8 assigned instances; this is a ceiling, not a target, and may be lowered for resource limits or I/O scheduling. The orchestrator checks its ledger before each assignment; the soft scheduling limit never overrides the hard total-instance cap.

Optional map/reduce scheduling: when useful, the orchestrator may define distinct, bounded map and reduce tasks over explicit inputs and outputs, directly assigning each to a different fresh instance. Independent reductions may run concurrently; schedule later reductions only when their dependencies are ready. Track the tasks and dependencies in the orchestrator-owned graph and ledger. This is guidance, not a requirement; a serial path is fine when partitioning does not help.

Soft I/O scheduling preference: when it is obvious that several tasks will compile or build concurrently, stagger their starts when practical (for example, tests that each trigger a compilation) to reduce I/O contention. This is not strict serialization: tolerate overlap when the expected penalty is small or coordination delay would cost more.

Maximize dependency-ready parallel assignments within approved scope and capacity. Prefer one worker per independently writable function, testcase, fixture, adapter, configuration slice, documentation section, or small semantic change. Do not split one tightly coupled edit merely to increase concurrency. Concurrent writes to one tracked file require isolated worktrees or patch boundaries and an explicit conflict/integration plan; otherwise use one active writer. Whenever a worker finishes or discovers separable work, reconsider decomposition and queue fresh direct assignments when prerequisites, checks, and integration remain clear.

Every direct assignment prompt must explicitly include:

1. Role, current approved stage, task ID, goal, orchestrator identity, task-owner/lead identity if distinct, and relevant approved inputs.
2. Allowed files, worktree/build directory, dependencies, acceptance criteria, focused validation commands, and prohibited actions.
3. Commit/integration owner and required return format: summary, evidence, changed files, commands with results, commit IDs or uncommitted status, blockers, risks, and next action.
4. The path to this contract and relevant repository instructions/skills; do not assume inherited context.
5. Model `MAI Code 2 Flash` with maximum supported effort (`reasoning-effort: max`). If unavailable, mark the task BLOCKED and do not use a fallback or silently substitute. Repeat exactly: "Use the maximum reasoning effort available. Think deeply and rigorously, examine assumptions and edge cases, and verify your conclusions before reporting."
6. Prefix every shell command with `date;`, inspect returned timestamps, and track elapsed time. Report elapsed time, progress, blockers, and next action approximately every five minutes or at the earliest opportunity after a blocking operation. If interim delivery is unsupported, return timestamped progress notes and disclose that live reporting was unavailable.
7. After three unsuccessful focused fix-and-check attempts on the same issue, escalate and stop its affected workflow line. Return attempted fixes, validation results, the remaining blocker, and recommendations. Do not begin a fourth attempt until the lead/orchestrator has reviewed the escalation and explicitly authorized a revised next action.
8. Put all temporary files under `/tmp/copilot`, preferably in task-specific subdirectories. Reading, writing, and deleting under `/tmp` is pre-approved; do not ask for permission. Limit cleanup to task-owned files. Set `TMPDIR` for task-owned tools when supported; disclose tool-managed outputs whose location cannot be controlled. Do not remove unrelated temporary files or change the user's global environment.

## Cloud, Network, and Workstation Policy

- Prefer cloud-hosted `MAI Code 2 Flash` agent instances for eligible independent research, planning, review, and implementation tasks when the environment provides approved workspace access. The orchestrator directly assigns the task and keeps the assigned lead accountable. If a cloud agent assignment is unavailable or unsuitable, mark the task BLOCKED and report the limitation; do not use a fallback model or claim a cloud task ran when it did not.
- Minimize transfer volume: send only the task prompt, relevant excerpts/diffs, and necessary test artifacts; reuse cached results and downloads; avoid duplicate repository or build uploads. Use only approved agent infrastructure for workspace data and never transmit secrets or private data to unapproved services. Tasks requiring local-only files, runtime, browser/device access, or hardware checks stay local unless an approved cloud agent can access that same environment.
- During ordinary slowness, avoid unnecessary requests and duplicate transfers.
- On a detected network interruption, pause all task work, including local and cloud work, at a safe checkpoint and preserve in-progress state. Resume only when passive recovery is indicated, a necessary ordinary network operation succeeds, or the user confirms recovery. Do not generate traffic solely to test connectivity. Record the pause, recovery signal, and resume point; do not claim remote checks passed while unavailable. If no recovery signal is available, remain paused.
- User-provided workstation profile: quad-core Intel i7, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB disk. These are total capacities, not free resources; do not assume a CPU generation, hyperthreading, or idle capacity. Before resource-heavy work, check current CPU, available memory, and free disk when observable. Cap CPU-heavy concurrency at four cores and reduce it to preserve responsiveness or when headroom is low. Apply the soft I/O preference to obvious concurrent builds without making overlap a hard failure. If resource data is unavailable, state that and choose conservative concurrency. This local capacity does not improve network speed.

## Git and Process Discipline

- Make frequent small commits after each cleared semantic block, including deliberate red-test checkpoints. Follow the stop-the-line protocol above before and after every task commit. Run focused validation and record its actual result; a known failing checkpoint must be labeled clearly. Do not hide failures or claim a commit is green when it is not.
- Assign one commit owner per worktree. Inspect the staged diff, stage only task-owned changes, and preserve pre-existing modifications. Workers without commit ownership return evidence to the owner rather than staging or committing.
- Parallel writers and incompatible build targets use isolated worktrees/build directories. Do not concurrently edit the same file or reconfigure a shared checkout. The orchestrator owns integration order, conflict resolution assignments, and post-integration validation.
- Every push requires fresh, explicit human approval for the exact remote, destination branch, and commit(s) or range. The preference to push early/often is not standing authorization. Do not push while approval is absent or ambiguous; report the proposed push and wait. After approval, push only the approved commits and report the result. Do not rewrite pushed history or run destructive git operations without separate explicit permission. Follow repository attribution rules for shared artifacts and commits.
- Reuse suitable existing processes. Record ownership, PIDs/terminal IDs, ports, revisions, and URLs as applicable. Stop unneeded task-owned processes before handoff; preserve user-owned processes and work.

## Ledger and Handoff

Keep task state under `/tmp/copilot/<task-id>/` unless the human requests a durable repository artifact. Use a concise ledger with task/stage, owner, dependencies, deliverable revision, validation evidence, QA verdict, human approval message/reference, commit IDs, blockers, and next action. Reconstruct approval evidence after interruption; never invent it. Share stage summaries in chat because temporary files are not durable records.

Finish only after code review, final QA, and human sign-off. Report changes, commits, validation and coverage gaps, unresolved risks explicitly accepted by the human, and remaining task-owned artifacts/processes. No automatic release or deployment is implied.

## Configuration Checks

Validate frontmatter with a YAML parser, unique role names, resolvable direct-assignment targets and contract links, explicit model/effort settings, terminal roles without agent-launch tools, the hard total cap of 8, and the soft concurrent-agent maximum of 8. Dry-run all six stages on a human-selected small task. Exercise the active-instance ledger at the hard cap and confirm it blocks an assignment that would exceed the cap; verify the soft maximum can be lowered for resource limits and is not treated as a target. Exercise normal single-attempt iteration, current-gate rejection, an escaped defect after gate approval, three-failure escalation, implementation-stage excessive ambiguity and human-directed reopening, expected-red tests, unavailable models, direct-assignment unavailability remaining BLOCKED, and scope changes. Verify test specifications and deterministic mock-data handoffs where appropriate. Exercise proposed-artifact review before Plan approval/advancement to Test Plan and rendered-result review after implementation before Code Review; include QA and human gates. For code/test stages, exercise owner-focused checks and independent Development Reviewer coverage at substeps without routine QA holds, followed by one aggregate stage QA review bound to the final commit range/hash; exercise the existing substep and commit QA cadence for non-code work. Also exercise a QA FAIL/repair loop without per-attempt QA, and an earlier scoped QA check only for an explicit request, pre-agreed risk trigger, or active escalation/Andon. Exercise a full pause on network interruption with recovery only on passive recovery, success of a necessary ordinary operation, or user confirmation; cloud assignment with minimal transfer; resource-limited scheduling, including the soft preference to stagger obvious concurrent compilation starts when practical without requiring strict serialization; and a proposed push that remains blocked until exact-scope human approval. Static checks do not replace runtime dry-run evidence.
